items.stimulus:
Text 1
Readers have long treated Agnes Marlowe's 1911 novel The Lexicographer's Daughter as a gentle family comedy. Its scenes of a father and daughter quarreling over word definitions are, in this view, light domestic sketches meant chiefly to amuse.

Text 2
Marlowe's novel is certainly funny. But its quarrels over definitions track a real debate of the period: whether dictionaries should record how people actually speak or dictate how they ought to. Beneath the comedy lies a serious argument about language.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel's dinner-table setting is its most carefully described location.
The novel's quarrels over word definitions are presented with humor.
The novel is meant mainly to amuse rather than to make an argument.
The novel takes part in a debate over the proper role of dictionaries.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the novel a comedy whose quarrels are meant to amuse, and Text 2 opens by granting that the novel 'is certainly funny.' That concession is the shared ground: both authors see the quarrels as humorous. They split over whether anything serious lies underneath.

A.why: You went to a detail from the novel itself instead of the critics' claims about it. Neither author says anything about how carefully any setting is described.

C.why: This is Text 1's view only. Text 2 rejects it and says the comedy covers a serious argument about language.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 describes the scenes as light sketches and never connects them to a debate about dictionaries.

Text 1
Hester Crane's 1894 poem cycle Loom Songs is usually read as a lament. Its speakers, young women in a cotton mill, describe the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours, and critics have taken the poems as straightforward protests against factory labor.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

Loom Songs is best understood as a simple protest against factory labor.
Loom Songs builds its strongest effects around the sound of the shuttle.
Loom Songs depicts the difficulties of working in a cotton mill.

A.why: This is Text 2's new claim. Text 1 reads the poems only as laments and protests and says nothing about pride in skill.

B.why: This is Text 1's reading, and Text 2 argues against it by saying the weavers are more than victims.

The following text is adapted from Ada Marlow's 1909 poem "Shuttle Song."
My shuttle runs like a swallow, / back and over, back and over; / the cloth grows under my hands / as a meadow greens in April. / Twelve strokes, and the bell; / twelve strokes, and the bell.

Text 2
"Shuttle Song" is often anthologized as a cheerful hymn to the loom, and its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness. Yet Marlow closes on a counted refrain tied to the mill bell. Beneath the borrowed countryside, the poem records labor measured out by someone else's clock.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The poem openly protests the harsh conditions of early mill labor.
The speaker describes her weaving with images taken from the countryside.
The poem is chiefly a cheerful celebration of working at the loom.
The speaker's pride in her cloth shows that weaving is fulfilling work.
items.explanation: Text 1 compares the shuttle to a swallow and the growing cloth to a meadow in April. Text 2 grants exactly this ('its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness') before it turns to the bell. Both authors accept that the poem uses countryside imagery for the work.

A.why: The critic finds the regimentation 'beneath' the imagery, which means it is hidden, not openly protested. The poem itself never complains.

C.why: Text 2 names this as the common reading and then disputes it, arguing that the bell refrain undercuts the cheer.

D.why: This is your own reading of the imagery, and the critic would not accept it. Text 2 argues that the sweetness hides labor controlled by 'someone else's clock.'

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Josiah Penrose's 1806 novel The Surgeon's House.
Dr. Lyle laid out his tables of cases, but Mrs. Hart only drew her son closer. Then Clara, the doctor's daughter, rolled back her sleeve, took the lancet, and made the small scratch herself. "It is no worse than a briar," she said. Mrs. Hart watched the girl's steady hand, then held out the boy's arm.

Text 2
Clara is usually celebrated as a heroine of the new science of vaccination. She is brave, certainly, but notice what actually moves Mrs. Hart: not the doctor's tables, which she ignores, but the sight of another person accepting the risk first. Penrose understood that trust, more than data, wins converts.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel suggests that medical evidence plays no part in medicine.
Mrs. Hart is persuaded mainly by the figures in Dr. Lyle's tables.
Mrs. Hart lets her son be vaccinated after watching Clara's act.
Mrs. Hart's hesitation is portrayed as a foolish superstition.
items.explanation: In Text 1, Mrs. Hart holds out her son's arm only after she watches Clara scratch her own. Text 2 points to the same moment as the thing that 'actually moves Mrs. Hart.' Both authors tie her decision to Clara's example.

A.why: You stretched the critic's 'more than data' into 'no part at all.' Text 2 ranks trust above evidence. It does not throw evidence out.

B.why: Both texts say the reverse: Mrs. Hart draws her son closer while the tables are laid out, and the critic says she ignores them.

D.why: You read Text 1 your own way instead of through the critic's frame. Neither text calls her caution foolish, and the critic treats it as something to win over with trust.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Ilse Marrow's Garden Suite (1894) is a set of parlor confections: seven brief pieces of pleasant melody, written for amateur pianists to play after dinner. Nothing in them asks to be remembered the next morning, and their very brevity shows that Marrow aimed only to charm her listeners.

Text 2
Granted, Marrow wrote the seven brief pieces of the Garden Suite for amateurs to play at home, and their melodies are easy to love. Yet nearly every piece ends on an unresolved chord, so the suite never comes to rest. That refusal quietly unsettles the very parlor the music was written to entertain.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The suite was composed for amateur performers in a home setting.
The melodies in the suite are appealing to listeners.
The suite's only purpose is to charm and entertain its listeners.
The suite is made up of several short pieces.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends on the claim that Marrow 'aimed only to charm,' and that last claim is what Text 2 answers. Text 2 grants that the suite was written for amateurs, that it has appealing melodies, and that its pieces are short. Then it turns: the unresolved endings 'unsettle' the parlor, so charm is not the suite's only purpose. Text 2's critic would reject this statement, so it is the one both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have read Text 2's 'Yet' as rejecting everything before it. But Text 2 opens with 'Granted, Marrow wrote... for amateurs to play at home,' so it accepts this point outright. Both authors agree with it.

B.why: You may have reasoned that a critic who finds the suite unsettling can't think it is pleasant. That comes from your own reading of the music, not from Text 2. Text 2 calls the melodies 'easy to love' and argues that the unease comes from the endings, not the tunes.

D.why: Both texts describe the suite as 'seven brief pieces.' Text 2 never disputes the brevity. It disputes only what Text 1 concludes from it.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Thomas Reeve's long poem The Husbandman's Year (1801) is, above all, a manual. Its twelve books follow the farming calendar month by month, and its advice on rotating turnips with barley is as sound as any treatise of the day. Scenes of village life lend color, but Reeve wrote in verse chiefly so that farmers would remember his lessons.

Text 2
Few would deny that the farming advice in The Husbandman's Year is accurate, or that its structure mirrors the agricultural calendar. Yet every book closes on a scene of open village fields that, by 1801, enclosure was fencing off. The poem is less a manual than a lament for a disappearing way of farming.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The poem's main purpose is to teach farmers practical methods.
The poem's advice about farming is accurate.
The poem includes scenes of village life as well as instruction.
The poem's structure follows the cycle of the farming year.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins with a concession ('Few would deny') that the advice is accurate and that the poem follows the calendar. It also builds its own argument on the poem's village scenes. Its main clause then rejects Text 1's central claim: the poem is 'less a manual than a lament.' The view that the poem's main purpose is instruction belongs to Text 1 alone, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

B.why: You may have assumed that a critic who calls the poem a lament must doubt its farming advice. Text 2 says outright that 'few would deny' the advice is accurate, so both authors accept this.

C.why: You may have dismissed this because Text 1 treats the village scenes as mere 'color.' The question asks only whether both authors would agree that the scenes are in the poem. They do agree, and in fact Text 2's whole reading depends on them.

D.why: Text 1 says the books 'follow the farming calendar month by month,' and Text 2 grants that the structure 'mirrors the agricultural calendar.' This is shared ground, not the point of disagreement.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Hana Ostrow's woodcut series Harbor Hours (1927) documents working life on the Baltic docks. Its twenty prints show stevedores hauling nets, coiling rope, and mending hulls, and every winch and cleat is cut with an engineer's precision. Ostrow plainly set out to preserve a faithful record of the dockworkers' labor.

Text 2
Certainly the tackle in Harbor Hours is cut with exacting care, and the series never leaves the docks. But Ostrow printed each block repeatedly, carving more away between printings, so that in the final impressions the workers sink into solid black. Read as a whole, the series records less the labor itself than its vanishing from view.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The series depicts people performing work at the docks.
Ostrow cut the equipment in the prints with great precision.
The series keeps its focus on the docks rather than elsewhere.
Ostrow's chief aim was to preserve a faithful record of dock labor.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends with the claim that Ostrow 'set out to preserve a faithful record,' and Text 2 is written to answer that sentence. Text 2 concedes the precise tackle and the dockside setting, and its own argument assumes the prints show workers. It then argues that the series records the labor's 'vanishing from view,' not the labor itself. A faithful record as Ostrow's chief aim is Text 1's view only, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have focused on the image of workers sinking into black and decided Text 2 denies that the prints show labor. But figures can only disappear from prints that show them in the first place. Both authors agree that the series depicts dockworkers.

B.why: Text 2's 'Certainly the tackle... is cut with exacting care' grants this point. The 'But' that follows challenges what the series means, not how carefully it was cut.

C.why: Text 1 sets every print on the docks, and Text 2 says the series 'never leaves the docks.' Both authors agree on this.
